CHAPTER XLIV.

EASE NOT PEACE.

    “A dull rotation, never at a stay,
     Yesterday’s face twin image of to-day.”
                     COWPER.

    “Of what each one should be, he sees the form and rule,
     And till he reach to that, his joy can ne’er be full.”
                    RÜCKERT.


It was very well for Margaret that the extreme quiet of the Harley
Street house, during Edith’s recovery from her confinement, gave her the
natural rest which she needed. It gave her time to comprehend the sudden
change which had taken place in her circumstances within the last two
months. She found herself at once an inmate of a luxurious house, where
the bare knowledge of the existence of every trouble or care seemed
scarcely to have penetrated. The wheels of the machinery of daily life
were well oiled, and went along with delicious smoothness. Mrs. Shaw and
Edith could hardly make enough of Margaret, on her return to what they
persisted in calling her home. And she felt that it was almost
ungrateful in her to have a secret feeling that the Helstone
vicarage—nay, even the poor little house at Milton, with her anxious
father and her invalid mother, and all the small household cares of
comparative poverty, composed her idea of home. Edith was impatient to
get well, in order to fill Margaret’s bed-room with all the soft
comforts, and pretty knick-knacks, with which her own abounded. Mrs.
Shaw and her maid found plenty of occupation in restoring Margaret’s
wardrobe to a state of elegant variety. Captain Lennox was easy, kind,
and gentlemanly; sate with his wife in her dressing-room an hour or two
every day; played with his little boy for another hour, and lounged away
the rest of his time at his club, when he was not engaged out to
dinner. Just before Margaret had recovered from her necessity for quiet
and repose—before she had begun to feel her life wanting and
dull—Edith came downstairs and resumed her usual part in the household;
and Margaret fell into the old habit of watching, and admiring, and
ministering to her cousin. She gladly took all charge of the semblances
of duties off Edith’s hands; answered notes, reminded her of
engagements, tended her when no gaiety was in prospect, and she was
consequently rather inclined to fancy herself ill. But all the rest of
the family were in the full business of the London season, and Margaret
was often left alone. Then her thoughts went back to Milton, with a
strange sense of the contrast between the life there, and here. She was
getting surfeited of the eventless ease in which no struggle or
endeavour was required. She was afraid lest she should even become
sleepily deadened into forgetfulness of anything beyond the life which
was lapping her round with luxury. There might be toilers and moilers
there in London, but she never saw them; the very servants lived in an
underground world of their own, of which she knew neither the hopes nor
the fears; they only seemed to start into existence when some want or
whim of their master and mistress needed them. There was a strange
unsatisfied vacuum in Margaret’s heart and mode of life; and, once when
she had dimly hinted this to Edith, the latter, wearied with dancing the
night before, languidly stroked Margaret’s cheek as she sat by her in
the old attitude,—she on a footstool by the sofa where Edith lay.

“Poor child!” said Edith. “It is a little sad for you to be left, night
after night, just at this time when all the world is so gay. But we
shall be having our dinner-parties soon—as soon as Henry comes back
from circuit—and then there will be a little pleasant variety for you.
No wonder it is moped, poor darling!”

Margaret did not feel as if the dinner-parties would be a panacea. But
Edith piqued herself on her dinner-parties; “so different,” as she said,
“from the old dowager dinners under mamma’s _régime_”; and Mrs. Shaw
herself seemed to take exactly the same kind of pleasure in the very
different arrangements and circle of acquaintances which were to Captain
and Mrs. Lennox’s taste, as she did in the more formal and ponderous
entertainments which she herself used to give. Captain Lennox was always
extremely kind and brotherly to Margaret. She was really very fond of
him, excepting when he was anxiously attentive to Edith’s dress and
appearance, with a view to her beauty making a sufficient impression on
the world. Then all the latent Vashti in Margaret was roused, and she
could hardly keep herself from expressing her feelings.

The course of Margaret’s day was this: a quiet hour or two before a late
breakfast; an unpunctual meal, lazily eaten by weary and half-awake
people, but yet at which, in all its dragged out length, she was
expected to be present, because, directly afterwards, came a discussion
of plans, at which, although they none of them concerned her, she was
expected to give her sympathy, if she could not assist with her advice;
an endless number of notes to write, which Edith invariably left to
her, with many caressing compliments as to her _eloquence du billet_; a
little play with Sholto as he returned from his morning’s walk; besides
the care of the children during the servants’ dinner; a drive or
callers; and some dinner or morning engagement for her aunt and cousins,
which left Margaret free, it is true, but rather wearied with the
inactivity of the day, coming upon depressed spirits and delicate
health.

She looked forward with longing, though unspoken interest to the homely
object of Dixon’s return from Milton; where, until now, the old servant
had been busily engaged in winding up all the affairs of the Hale
family. It had appeared a sudden famine to her heart, this entire
cessation of any news respecting the people among whom she had lived so
long. It was true, that Dixon, in her business-like letters, quoted,
every now and then, an opinion of Mr. Thornton’s as to what she had
better do about the furniture, or how act in regard to the landlord of
the Crampton Terrace house. But it was only here and there that the name
came in, or any Milton name, indeed; and Margaret was sitting one
evening, all alone in the Lennox’s drawing-room, not reading Dixon’s
letters, which yet she held in her hand, but thinking over them, and
recalling the days which had been, and picturing the busy life out of
which her own had been taken and never missed; wondering if all went on
in that whirl just as if she and her father had never been; questioning
within herself, if no one in all the crowd missed her (not Higgins, she
was not thinking of him), when, suddenly Mr. Bell was announced; and
Margaret hurried the letters into her work-basket, and started up,
blushing as if she had been doing some guilty thing.

“Oh, Mr. Bell! I never thought of seeing you!”

“But you give me a welcome, I hope, as well as that very pretty start of
surprise.”

“Have you dined? How did you come? Let me order you some dinner.”

“If you’re going to have any. Otherwise, you know, there is no one who
cares less for eating than I do. But where are the others? Gone out to
dinner? Left you alone?”

“Oh yes! and it is such a rest. I was just thinking—But will you run
the risk of dinner? I don’t know if there is anything in the house.”

“Why, to tell you the truth, I dined at my club. Only they don’t cook as
well as they did, so I thought, if you were going to dine, I might try
and make out my dinner. But never mind, never mind! There aren’t ten
cooks in England to be trusted at impromptu dinners. If their skill and
their fires will stand it, their tempers won’t. You shall make me some
tea, Margaret. And now, what were you thinking of? you were going to
tell me. Whose letters were those, god-daughter, that you hid away so
speedily?”

“Only Dixon’s,” replied Margaret, growing very red.

“Whew! is that all? Who do you think came up in the train with me?”

“I don’t know,” said Margaret, resolved against making a guess.

“Your what d’ye call him? What’s the right name for a cousin-in-law’s
brother?”

“Mr. Henry Lennox?” asked Margaret.

“Yes,” replied Mr. Bell. “You knew him formerly, didn’t you? What sort
of a person is he, Margaret?”

“I liked him long ago,” said Margaret, glancing down for a moment. And
then she looked straight up and went on in her natural manner. “You know
we have been corresponding about Frederick since; but I have not seen
him for nearly three years, and he may be changed. What did you think of
him?”

“I don’t know. He was so busy trying to find out who I was, in the first
instance, and what I was in the second, that he never let out what he
was; unless indeed that veiled curiosity of his as to what manner of man
he had to talk to was not a good piece, and a fair indication of his
character. Do you call him good-looking, Margaret?”

“No! certainly not. Do you?”

“Not I. But I thought perhaps you might. Is he a great deal here?”

“I fancy he is when he is in town. He has been on circuit now since I
came. But—Mr. Bell—have you come from Oxford or from Milton?”

“From Milton. Don’t you see I’m smoke-dried?”

“Certainly. But I thought that it might be the effect of the antiquities
of Oxford.”

“Come now, be a sensible woman! In Oxford, I could have managed all the
landlords in the place, and had my own way, with half the trouble your
Milton landlord has given me, and defeated me after all. He won’t take
the house off our hands till next June twelve-month. Luckily, Mr.
Thornton found a tenant for it. Why don’t you ask after Mr. Thornton,
Margaret? He has proved himself a very active friend of yours, I can
tell you. Taken more than half the trouble off my hands.”

“And how is he? How is Mrs. Thornton?” asked Margaret hurriedly and
below her breath, though she tried to speak out.

“I suppose they’re well. I’ve been staying at their house till I was
driven out of it by the perpetual clack about that Thornton girl’s
marriage. It was too much for Thornton himself, though she was his
sister. He used to go and sit in his own room perpetually. He’s getting
past the age for caring for such things, either as principal or
accessory. I was surprised to find the old lady falling into the
current, and carried away by her daughter’s enthusiasm for
orange-blossoms and lace. I thought Mrs. Thornton had been made of
sterner stuff.”

“She would put on any assumption of feeling to veil her daughter’s
weakness,” said Margaret in a low voice.

“Perhaps so. You’ve studied her, have you? She doesn’t seem over fond of
you, Margaret.”

“I know it,” said Margaret. “Oh, here is tea, at last!” exclaimed she,
as if relieved. And with tea came Mr. Henry Lennox, who had walked up to
Harley Street after a late dinner, and had evidently expected to find
his brother and sister-in-law at home. Margaret suspected him of being
as thankful as she was at the presence of a third party, on this their
first meeting since the memorable day of his offer, and her refusal at
Helstone. She could hardly tell what to say at first, and was thankful
for all the tea-table occupations, which gave her an excuse for keeping
silence, and him an opportunity for recovering himself. For, to tell the
truth, he had rather forced himself up to Harley Street this evening,
with a view of getting over an awkward meeting, awkward even in the
presence of Captain Lennox and Edith, and doubly awkward now that he
found her the only lady there, and the person to whom he must naturally
and perforce address a great part of his conversation. She was the first
to recover her self-possession. She began to talk on the subject which
came uppermost in her mind, after the first flush of awkward shyness.

“Mr. Lennox, I have been so much obliged to you for all you have done
about Frederick.”

“I am only sorry it has been so unsuccessful,” replied he, with a quick
glance towards Mr. Bell, as if reconnoitring how much he might say
before him. Margaret, as if she read his thought, addressed herself to
Mr. Bell, both including him in the conversation, and implying that he
was perfectly aware of the endeavours that had been made to clear
Frederick.

“That Horrocks—that very last witness of all, has proved as unavailing
as all the others. Mr. Lennox has discovered that he sailed for
Australia only last August; only two months before Frederick was in
England, and gave us the names of——”

“Frederick in England! you never told me that!” exclaimed Mr. Bell in
surprise.

“I thought you knew. I never doubted you had been told. Of course, it
was a great secret, and perhaps I should not have named it now,” said
Margaret, a little dismayed.

“I have never named it to either my brother or your cousin,” said Mr.
Lennox, with a little professional dryness of implied reproach.

“Never mind, Margaret. I am not living in a talking, babbling world, nor
yet among people who are trying to worm facts out of me; you needn’t
look so frightened because you have let the cat out of the bag to a
faithful old hermit like me. I shall never name his having been in
England; I shall be out of temptation, for no one will ask me. Stay!”
(interrupting himself rather abruptly). “Was it at your mother’s
funeral?”

“He was with mamma when she died,” said Margaret, softly.

“To be sure! To be sure! Why, some one asked me if he had not been over
then, and I denied it stoutly—not many weeks ago—who could it have
been? Oh! I recollect!”

But he did not say the name; and although Margaret would have given much
to know if her suspicions were right, and it had been Mr. Thornton who
had made the enquiry, she could not ask the question of Mr. Bell, much
as she longed to do so.

There was a pause for a moment or two. Then Mr. Lennox said, addressing
himself to Margaret, “I suppose as Mr. Bell is now acquainted with all
the circumstances attending your brother’s unfortunate dilemma, I cannot
do better than inform him exactly how the research into the evidence we
once hoped to produce in his favour stands at present. So, if he will do
me the honour to breakfast with me to-morrow, we will go over the names
of these missing gentry.”

“I should like to hear all the particulars, if I may. Cannot you come
here? I dare not ask you both to breakfast, though I am sure you would
be welcome. But let me know all you can about Frederick, even though
there may be no hope at present.”

“I have an engagement at half-past eleven. But I will certainly come if
you wish it,” replied Mr. Lennox with a little after-thought of extreme
willingness, which made Margaret shrink into herself, and almost wish
that she had not proposed her natural request. Mr. Bell got up and
looked around him for his hat, which had been removed to make room for
tea.

“Well!” said he, “I don’t know what Mr. Lennox is inclined to do, but
I’m disposed to be moving off homewards. I’ve been a journey to-day, and
journeys begin to tell upon my sixty and odd years.”

“I believe I shall stay and see my brother and sister,” said Mr. Lennox,
making no movement of departure. Margaret was seized with a shy awkward
dread of being left alone with him. The scene on the little terrace in
the Helstone garden was so present to her, that she could hardly help
believing it was so with him.

“Don’t go yet, please Mr. Bell,” said she, hastily. “I want you to see
Edith; and I want Edith to know you. Please!” said she, laying a light
but determined hand on his arm. He looked at her, and saw the confusion
stirring in her countenance; he sate down again, as if her little touch
had been possessed of resistless strength.

“You see how she overpowers me, Mr. Lennox,” said he. “And I hope you
noticed the happy choice of her expressions; she wants me to ‘see’ this
cousin Edith, who, I am told, is a great beauty; but she has the honesty
to change her word when she comes to me—Mrs. Lennox is to ‘know’ me. I
suppose I am not much to ‘see,’ eh, Margaret?”

He joked, to give her time to recover from the slight flutter which he
had detected in her manner on his proposal to leave; and she caught the
tone, and threw the ball back. Mr. Lennox wondered how his brother, the
Captain, could have reported her as having lost all her good looks. To
be sure, in her quiet black dress, she was a contrast to Edith, dancing
in her white crape mourning, and long floating golden hair, all softness
and glitter. She dimpled and blushed most becomingly when introduced to
Mr. Bell, conscious that she had her reputation as a beauty to keep up,
and that it would not do to have a Mordecai refusing to worship and
admire, even in the shape of an old Fellow of a College, which nobody
had ever heard of. Mrs. Shaw and Captain Lennox, each in their separate
way, gave Mr. Bell a kind and sincere welcome, winning him over to like
them almost in spite of himself, especially when he saw how naturally
Margaret took her place as sister and daughter of the house.

“What a shame that we were not at home to receive you,” said Edith.
“You, too, Henry! though I don’t know that we should have stayed at home
for you. And for Mr. Bell! for Margaret’s Mr. Bell——”

“There is no knowing what sacrifices you would not have made,” said her
brother-in-law. “Even a dinner-party! and the delight of wearing this
very becoming dress.”

Edith did not know whether to frown or to smile, but it did not suit Mr.
Lennox to drive her to the first of these alternatives; so he went on.

“Will you show your readiness to make sacrifices to-morrow morning,
first by asking me to breakfast, to meet Mr. Bell, and secondly, by
being so kind as to order it at half-past nine, instead of at ten
o’clock? I have some letters and papers that I want to show to Miss Hale
and Mr. Bell.”

“I hope Mr. Bell will make our house his own during his stay in London,”
said Captain Lennox. “I am only so sorry we cannot offer him a bedroom.”

“Thank you. I am much obliged to you. You would only think me a churl if
you had, for I should decline it, I believe, in spite of all the
temptations of such agreeable company,” said Mr. Bell, bowing all round,
and secretly congratulating himself on the neat turn he had given to his
sentence, which, if put into plain language, would have been more to
this effect: “I couldn’t stand the restraints of such a proper-behaved
and civil-spoken people as these are: it would be like meat without
salt. I’m thankful they haven’t a bed. And how well I rounded my
sentence! I’m absolutely catching the trick of good manners.”

His self-satisfaction lasted him till he was fairly out in the streets,
walking side by side with Henry Lennox. Here he suddenly remembered
Margaret’s little look of entreaty as she urged him to stay longer, and
he also recollected a few hints given him long ago by an acquaintance of
Mr. Lennox’s, as to his admiration of Margaret. It gave a new direction
to his thoughts. “You have known Miss Hale for a long time, I believe.
How do you think her looking? She strikes me as pale and ill.”

“I thought her looking remarkably well. Perhaps not when I first
came—now I think of. But certainly, when she grew animated, she looked
as well as ever I saw her do.”

“She has had a great deal to go through,” said Mr. Bell.

“Yes! I have been sorry to hear of all she has had to bear; not merely
the common and universal sorrow arising from death, but all the
annoyance which her father’s conduct must have caused her, and then——”

“Her father’s conduct!” said Mr. Bell, in an accent of surprise. “You
must have heard some wrong statement. He behaved in the most
conscientious manner. He showed more resolute strength than I should
ever have given him credit for formerly.”

“Perhaps I have been wrongly informed. But I have been told, by his
successor in the living—a clever sensible man, and a thoroughly active
clergyman—that there was no call upon Mr. Hale to do what he did,
relinquish the living, and throw himself and his family on the tender
mercies of private teaching in a manufacturing town; the bishop had
offered him another living, it is true, but if he had come to entertain
certain doubts, he could have remained where he was, and so had no
occasion to resign. But the truth is, these country clergymen live such
isolated lives—isolated, I mean, from all intercourse with men of equal
cultivation with themselves, by whose minds they might regulate their
own, and discover when they were going either too fast or too slow—that
they are very apt to disturb themselves with imaginary doubts as to the
articles of faith, and throw up certain opportunities of doing good for
very uncertain fancies of their own.”

“I differ from you. I do not think they are very apt to do as my poor
friend Hale did.” Mr. Bell was inwardly chafing.

“Perhaps I used too general an expression in saying ‘very apt.’ But
certainly, their lives are such as very often to produce either
inordinate self-sufficiency, or a morbid state of conscience,” replied
Mr. Lennox with perfect coolness.

“You don’t meet with any self-sufficiency among the lawyers, for
instance?” asked Mr. Bell. “And seldom, I imagine, any cases of morbid
conscience.” He was becoming more and more vexed, and forgetting his
lately-caught trick of good manners. Mr. Lennox saw now that he had
annoyed his companion; and as he had talked pretty much for the sake of
saying something, and so passing the time away while their road lay
together, he was very indifferent as to the exact side he took upon the
question, and quietly came round by saying: “To be sure, there is
something fine in a man of Mr. Hale’s age leaving his home of twenty
years, and giving up all settled habits, for an idea which was probably
erroneous—but that does not matter—an untangible thought. One cannot
help admiring him, with a mixture of pity in one’s admiration, something
like what one feels for Don Quixote. Such a gentleman as he was too! I
shall never forget the refined and simple hospitality he showed to me
that last day at Helstone.”

Only half-mollified, and yet anxious, in order to lull certain qualms of
his own conscience, to believe that Mr. Hale’s conduct had a tinge of
Quixotism in it, Mr. Bell growled out—“Aye! And you don’t know Milton.
Such a change from Helstone! It is years since I have been at
Helstone—but I’ll answer for it, it is standing there yet—every stick
and every stone as it has done for the last century, while Milton! I go
there every four or five years—and I was born there—yet I do assure
you, I often lose my way—aye, among the very piles of warehouses that
are built upon my father’s orchard. Do we part here? Well, good-night,
sir; I suppose we shall meet in Harley Street to-morrow morning.”

The deep, unbroken quiet of the Harley Street house, while Edith recovered from her confinement, was a gentle blessing to Margaret Hale. It gave her the slow, unhurried rest her overstrained nerves had craved, and space to wrap her head around the staggering shift in her circumstances that had unfolded over the past two months. She found herself lodged in a home of such unsparing luxury that the very existence of hardship or small, grinding cares seemed never to have crossed its threshold. The cogs of daily life were so perfectly oiled that every routine turned with soft, unjarring smoothness. Mrs. Shaw and Edith fussed over her endlessly, insisting that this house was her true home now, and Margaret could not shake the faint, guilty secret that it did not feel like home at all: her idea of belonging was still tied to the sun-dappled Helstone vicarage, even to the cramped, drafty little cottage in Milton, with her anxious father, her ailing mother, and all the tiny, messy household troubles of their modest means.

Edith could barely wait to regain her strength before she set about refurnishing Margaret’s bedroom with the same heap of silk cushions, laced trinkets, and tiny porcelain curios that crowded every surface of her own chambers. Mrs. Shaw and her lady’s maid spent days restyling Margaret’s wardrobe, restoring it to an elegant, cheerful variety that suited the London season. Captain Lennox, meanwhile, was easy, kind, and unfailingly gentlemanly: he sat with Edith in her dressing room for an hour or two every day, played with his infant son Sholto for another, and lounged away the rest of his hours at his club or at dinner engagements with his fellow officers.

Just before Margaret had begun to chafe at the lack of purpose in her days, Edith came downstairs to resume her place at the head of the household, and Margaret fell back into the old familiar habit of tending to her cousin. She happily took all the trivial tedious duties off Edith’s hands: answered every social note, reminded her of forgotten calls, and sat by her side to soothe her when no gala was on the calendar and she felt languid enough to fancy herself ill. But the rest of the family was swept up entirely in the whirl of the London Season, and Margaret was often left entirely alone.

Her thoughts drifted back to Milton, and she was struck by the stark, unbridgeable contrast between that life and this one. She was growing sick of this eventless, effortless ease, where no struggle, no small act of meaningful work, was ever required. She feared she would grow sleepy and dull, forgetting every part of the world beyond the soft luxury that wrapped around her. There were toilers and drudges in London, she knew, but she never saw them: the servants lived in an invisible, underground world of their own, whose hopes and fears she would never learn, and they only seemed to spring into existence when a master or mistress rang a bell to satisfy some small want or whim. A strange, unsatisfied hollow yawned in Margaret’s chest, and once, when she hinted at this vague emptiness to Edith, the latter, still languid from dancing until three the night before, stroked Margaret’s cheek idly as she perched on a footstool beside the sofa where Edith lay.

“Poor child!” Edith said. “It’s so sad for you to be left home night after night just when all the world is at its gayest. But we’ll be hosting our dinner parties soon—just as soon as Henry comes back from circuit—and then you’ll have all sorts of nice little variety. No wonder you’re moped, poor darling.”

Margaret did not believe a string of dinner parties could fix that hollow feeling. But Edith prided herself on her dinner spreads, insisting they were nothing like the old stuffy, formal dowager dinners her mother used to host, and Mrs. Shaw herself took just as much delight in the Lennoxes’ bright, lively social circle as she had once taken in her own heavy, old-fashioned entertainments. Captain Lennox was unfailingly kind and brotherly to Margaret, and she was very fond of him—save for those rare moments when he fussed over Edith’s dress and appearance, determined that her beauty should dazzle every guest in the room. Then all the fiery, independent core of Margaret’s nature rose up, and she bit her tongue to keep from speaking her mind.

Her days unfolded in a lazy, unchanging rhythm: an hour or two of quiet before a late breakfast that no one bothered to serve punctually, eaten slowly by half-asleep, groggy people, where she was expected to sit through every dragged-out minute even though none of the family’s upcoming plans concerned her, expected to offer sympathy even if she could not offer advice. After that, there were endless stacks of notes Edith left for her to write, heaping soft compliments on Margaret’s elegant, charming letter-writing. She would play with Sholto after his morning walk, mind him while the servants ate their own dinner, go for a drive or receive callers, and then her aunt and cousins would head off to some engagement, leaving her free—yet tired, listless, her already delicate health worsened by days of no real work or purpose.

She waited, unspoken but longingly, for Dixon to return from Milton, where the old servant had been busy wrapping up every last one of the Hale family’s affairs. The total lack of news from the place she had called home for two years had felt like a famine to her. Dixon’s formal, businesslike letters only dropped in the stray mention of Mr. Thornton’s advice, about what to do with the Hale’s old furniture, or how to negotiate with the landlord of their Crampton Terrace cottage. Hardly any other Milton names ever crossed the page. One evening, she sat alone in the Lennox drawing room, holding Dixon’s half-read letters in her hand, staring into space as she thought back over old days, picturing Milton’s noisy, busy streets, wondering if that whole whirl went on just the same as if her and her father had never existed at all, wondering if anyone in that whole crowd missed her (not Higgins—she was not thinking of him at all) when the servant announced Mr. Bell. Margaret stuffed the letters into her workbasket in a hurry, and stood up blushing as if she had been caught doing something guilty.

“Oh, Mr. Bell! I never thought I would see you here!”
“I hope that surprised little start is paired with a proper welcome,” he laughed. “Have you dined? How did you get here? Let me order you something to eat at once,” Margaret fussed.
“Only if you’re planning to dine too. Otherwise, you know no one cares less about eating than I do. But where are all the rest? Gone out to dinner? Left you all alone?”
“Oh yes, and it’s such a quiet, lovely rest. I was just thinking—would you chance an impromptu dinner? I’ve no idea what’s in the larder.”
“To tell you the truth, I already dined at my club. Their cooks aren’t half as good as they used to be, though, so I thought if you were going to eat I might make a second go of it. Never mind, never mind! There aren’t ten cooks in all of England you can trust with an unexpected meal. Their skills and their fires might hold, but their tempers certainly won’t. You can make me tea instead, Margaret. Now—what were you thinking about, just now? You were going to tell me. Whose letters were those you hid away so fast, my god-daughter?”
“Only Dixon’s,” Margaret said, flushing bright.
“Whew! That’s all? Do you know who rode up from Milton in the same train as me today?”
“I’ve no idea,” Margaret said, refusing to guess.
“Your what-d’ye-call-him? The brother of your cousin-in-law? Henry Lennox?”
“Mr. Henry Lennox?” Margaret asked.
“That’s him,” Mr. Bell said. “You knew him long ago, didn’t you? What do you make of him, Margaret?”
“I liked him a very long time ago,” Margaret said, glancing down for a moment, then lifting her eyes to speak in her usual steady tone. “We’ve been corresponding about Frederick for years after that, but I haven’t seen him for nearly three. He might be quite changed now. What did you think of him?”
“I’m not sure. He was so busy trying to work out who I was, first, then what sort of status I held, that he never let a single thing slip about himself—unless all that veiled curiosity about the man he was talking to is a fair marker of his character. Do you think he’s good-looking, Margaret?”
“Certainly not,” she said. “Do you?”
“Not a bit. I thought you might, though. Is he often down here in town?”
“I think he is, when he’s not out on circuit. He’s been away on circuit ever since I arrived. But—Mr. Bell—did you come straight from Oxford, or from Milton?”
“From Milton. Can’t you see I’m still smoke-dried from the mills?”
“I did wonder if it might be all that ancient Oxford dust clinging to you,” Margaret teased.
“Come now, be sensible! In Oxford I could cajole every landlord in the city to give me my way with half the trouble your Milton landlord has given me—beaten me in the end, too. He won’t release our lease on the Crampton Terrace house until next June twelvemonth. Luckily, Mr. Thornton tracked down a new tenant for it for us. Why don’t you ask after Mr. Thornton, Margaret? He’s been a wonderfully active friend to you, you know. Took more than half the whole mess of work off my shoulders.”
“How is he? How is Mrs. Thornton?” Margaret asked, breathless, voice so quiet it was almost a murmur before she forced herself to speak louder.
“They’re well enough, as far as I can tell. I was staying at their house until I was driven half mad by nonstop chatter about the Thornton girl’s wedding. It was too much for Thornton himself, even though she’s his own sister. He kept escaping to lock himself in his study, the whole time. He’s far too old to care for all that frippery nonsense, either as the guest of honor or a bystander. I was shocked to see old Mrs. Thornton get swept up in the whole fuss, all her daughter’s glee over orange blossoms and lace carrying her away. I thought she was made of far sterner stuff.”
“She would put on any show of soft sentiment to hide her daughter’s silliness,” Margaret said softly. “You’re right, she doesn’t much care for me.”
“I know that for a fact,” Mr. Bell nodded.
“Oh, thank goodness, tea is here at last!” Margaret exclaimed, grateful for the interruption.

And with the tea came Henry Lennox himself, who had walked up to Harley Street after a late dinner, evidently expecting to find his brother and Edith at home. Margaret suspected he was just as relieved as she was to have a third party in the room: this was their first meeting since the fateful afternoon on the Helstone garden terrace, when he had proposed and she had turned him down. She did not know what to say at first, and was glad for all the little tea-table tasks to keep her hands busy and her mouth still, giving him time to collect himself too. He had forced himself to walk over tonight, after all, just to get this awkward first meeting over with—awkward even if the rest of the family had been home, and twice as awkward now that Margaret was the only other person in the room, the one he would naturally have to address most of his conversation to.

Margaret was the first to regain her composure. Once the initial flush of awkward shyness faded, she spoke of the first thing that came to her mind. “Mr. Lennox, I cannot thank you enough for all the work you’ve done on Frederick’s behalf.”
“I only wish it had been more successful,” he replied, glancing quickly over at Mr. Bell, as if gauging how much he could safely say in front of a stranger. Margaret read his thought instantly, and turned to Mr. Bell, drawing him clearly into the conversation, making it plain he knew every detail of the efforts to clear Frederick’s name.
“That last witness, Horrocks—the very last one we held out hope for—proved to be no help at all. Mr. Lennox found out he sailed for Australia last August, just two months before Frederick came back to England, and gave us all the names of—”
“Frederick was in England? No one ever told me that!” Mr. Bell exclaimed, shocked.
“I thought you knew. I never doubted someone must have mentioned it. Of course it was a great secret—perhaps I ought not to have said it now,” Margaret said, a little dismayed.
“I never named it to my brother, or your cousin, for that matter,” Mr. Lennox said, with the cool, dry tone of a professional who guarded his clients’ secrets.
“Never you mind, Margaret,” Mr. Bell said. “I don’t live in a gossiping, prying world, and none of my acquaintances go digging for hidden facts. You don’t have to look so frightened spilling the secret to an old hermit like me. I’ll never tell a soul he was here—no one will even ask me. Wait a minute!” he interrupted himself, suddenly sharp. “Was he here for your mother’s funeral?”
“He was with her when she died,” Margaret said softly.
“Of course! Of course! Someone asked me not many weeks ago if he hadn’t come over then, and I denied it stoutly—who was that? Oh, I remember!” He did not say the name, and Margaret ached to know if her suspicion was right, if it had been Mr. Thornton who had asked after Frederick—but she could not bring herself to pose the question.

There was a short, quiet pause. Then Mr. Lennox turned back to Margaret. “Since Mr. Bell now knows every circumstance of your brother’s unfortunate predicament, there is no better way forward than to walk him through exactly what remains of the evidence we once hoped to produce in his favor. If he would do me the honor of breakfasting with me tomorrow, we can go over every name of those missing witnesses.”
“I want to hear every last detail too, if I may. Can’t you both come here instead? I don’t quite dare formally invite you both to breakfast, but I know you would be more than welcome. I need to know everything we still can about Frederick, even if there is no hope of clearing him right now.”
“I have an appointment at half past eleven. But I will certainly come if you wish it,” Mr. Lennox replied, with a faint, unmissable eagerness that made Margaret draw back shyly, almost wishing she had not made the natural request.

Mr. Bell got to his feet, hunting for his hat that the servant had moved to make room for the tea tray. “Well, I don’t know what Mr. Lennox intends to do, but I’m for heading home. I’ve traveled all day, and long journeys start to wear on a man of sixty odd years.”
“I think I shall stay and wait for my brother and Edith to get back,” Mr. Lennox said, making no move to leave. A sudden, shy panic seized Margaret at the thought of being left alone with him. The memory of that afternoon on the Helstone terrace was so vivid to her, she could only assume it was just as vivid for him.
“Don’t go yet, please Mr. Bell,” she said quickly, laying a light, firm hand on his arm. “I want you to meet Edith. Please stay.” He looked at her, saw the flustered confusion stirring in her face, and sat down again at once, as if that small touch had held a strength he could not resist.
“You see how she overpowers me, Mr. Lennox,” he laughed. “And did you notice how cleverly she phrased it? First she said she wanted me to come ‘see’ her cousin Edith, the great beauty everyone talks about, but then she corrected herself to say Edith should ‘know’ me. I suppose I’m not much worth looking at, eh Margaret?” He joked to give her time to settle her frayed nerves, and she caught his light tone and bantered back easily. Mr. Lennox found himself wondering how his brother the Captain could ever have claimed Margaret had lost all her good looks. Dressed in her quiet black mourning gown, she was the perfect contrast to Edith, who drifted in a little later in her white crape mourning dress with loose golden curls floating around her shoulders, all softness and glitter. Edith dimpled and blushed prettily when she was introduced to Mr. Bell, determined to live up to her reputation as a great beauty and win over even this gruff old Oxford don. Mrs. Shaw and Captain Lennox both welcomed Mr. Bell warmly, and he found himself liking them almost against his will, especially when he saw how naturally Margaret slipped into her place as a beloved sister and daughter of the house.

“It is such a shame we were not home to greet you,” Edith said. “You too, Henry! Though I don’t know if we would have skipped our dinner party for you. But for Mr. Bell! For Margaret’s Mr. Bell—”
“There is no limit to the sacrifices you would have made,” her brother-in-law cut in, dry. “You would have skipped the whole gala, missed the chance to wear this very lovely dress, no doubt.” Edith did not know whether to frown or smile, and Henry Lennox was quick to turn the joke light before he irritated her. “Would you be willing to make a small sacrifice tomorrow morning, then? First, agree to host the breakfast to meet Mr. Bell, and second, make it half past nine instead of ten o’clock? I have a stack of letters and papers I want to show Miss Hale and Mr. Bell.”
“Please make our house your own for the whole duration of your stay in London,” Captain Lennox said to Mr. Bell. “I am only sorry we cannot offer you a bedroom for the night.”
“Thank you, I am much obliged. And I would be a churl if you did, because I should have to turn you down, even for the pleasure of such agreeable company,” Mr. Bell replied, bowing politely all around. Privately he congratulated himself on the well-turned phrase, when the plain truth of it was: I could not stand the stuffy, over-polite restraints of this household. It would be like eating meat without salt. I am thankful they have no spare bed.
